title: Combo Limits
subtitle: Pick the right tool for each limit.

questions.text: For $lim[x->a] f(x)$ to exist, $f(x)$ must be defined at $x = a$.
questions.explain: A limit ignores the point itself.

questions.text: If $lim[x->2] f(x) = 0$ and $lim[x->2] g(x) = 0$, then $lim[x->2] frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ does not exist.
questions.explain: $frac{0}{0}$ is indeterminate; it can be anything.

questions.text: If $p$ is a polynomial, then $lim[x->a] p(x) = p(a)$.
questions.explain: Direct substitution.

questions.text: If $lim[x->a] (f(x) - g(x))$ exists, then it must equal $lim[x->a] f(x) - lim[x->a] g(x)$.
questions.explain: $f$ and $g$ might not have limits on their own (like $frac{1}{x}$ and $frac{1}{x}$).
The bottom goes to $9 - 6 - 4 = -1 ≠ 0$, so the quotient law applies.

questions.text: $lim[x->2] sin(g(x)) = sin(lim[x->2] g(x))$, if $lim[x->2] g(x)$ exists.
questions.explain: Sine is continuous, so the limit passes inside.

questions.text: If you plug in and get $frac{a}{0}$, this is an "indeterminate form" and could be any number.
questions.explain: $frac{a}{0}$ with $a ≠ 0$ is an infinite limit or DNE. Only $frac{0}{0}$ is indeterminate.
It is 0.

slides.text: Every limit starts the same way: **plug in**. You get one of three things. Which one means you are done?
slides.hint: Which one is already an answer?
slides.explain: A number is the limit. $frac{a}{0}$ means an infinite limit or DNE. $frac{0}{0}$ means use a trick.

slides.text: Plugging in gives $frac{0}{0}$. Match the clue to the trick: the expression has a **square root**.
